Paper: Amirrajab et al. (2022). Label-informed cardiac MR image synthesis through conditional GANs. Comput Med Imaging Graph.
What it does: Generates cardiac MR images from segmentation label maps, so each image comes with a matching mask.
Conditioned on: Segmentation masks (anatomy only; no patient information).
How it was evaluated: Image similarity (SSIM, PSNR, NRMSE) and segmentation performance.
Main finding: The SPADE version beat Pix2Pix and Pix2PixHD baselines on image similarity.
Limits / gaps: Controls anatomy, not who the patient is. Privacy benefit is argued, not tested.
Why it matters for my thesis: The closest published version of your baseline (mask-conditioned generation).
How well I checked it: Via the Simula survey table only. That row merges this paper with Khalil et al. 2023, so read the original before quoting any numbers.

Paper: Amirrajab et al. (2023). Pathology synthesis of 3D-consistent cardiac MR images using 2D VAEs and GANs. Mach Learn Biomed Imaging.
What it does: Changes a mask's shape to create disease-like anatomy (for example hypertrophy or dilation), then turns the mask into an image.
Conditioned on: Segmentation masks that have been altered towards a pathology.
Model: Two stages: a VAE changes the mask, a label-conditioned GAN makes the image.
How it was evaluated: Distribution of end-diastolic and end-systolic volumes, Dice, Hausdorff distance.
Main finding: Helped segmentation generalise across vendors and to pathologies that were scarce in the data.
Limits / gaps: Conditions on disease shape, not on a broader clinical profile. No privacy evaluation reported.
Why it matters for my thesis: Shows you can steer disease-related anatomy. Your work steers it with patient information instead.
How well I checked it: Via the Simula survey table only.

Paper: Diller et al. (2020). Utility of deep learning networks for the generation of artificial cardiac MR images in congenital heart disease. BMC Med Imaging.
What it does: Trains one generator only on patients with Tetralogy of Fallot, then uses its images to train a segmentation network.
Conditioned on: Nothing (unconditional), but the training cohort is one specific disease.
How it was evaluated: Expert review and Dice against ground-truth masks.
Main finding: A segmentation network trained on the synthetic images came within 1% of one trained on real data.
Limits / gaps: No control over who is generated. Privacy benefit stated, not measured.
Why it matters for my thesis: Evidence that synthetic data can stand in for a small, rare-disease cohort.
How well I checked it: Via the Simula survey table only.

Paper: Campello et al. (2022). Cardiac aging synthesis from cross-sectional data with conditional GANs. Front Cardiovasc Med.
What it does: Makes an older or younger version of a given heart scan. Also changes apparent BMI.
Conditioned on: Age (or BMI) as the gap between the scan's current value and the target value.
Model: Conditional GAN (WGAN-GP) with a U-Net generator, residual and attention blocks, and sinusoidal embedding of the covariate.
Data: UK Biobank. 43,352 participants available; 14,788 used for training. Four-chamber view, end-diastole, 2D, 128x128.
How it was evaluated: Image quality (FID, PSNR). Age error from a separately trained age regressor. LV size, septum width and ejection fraction from segmentations. Data augmentation test.
Main finding: Changes concentrated in the interventricular septum and aorta. Adding 10 to 25% synthetic scans brought age-prediction error close to a balanced dataset.
Limits / gaps: Not checked against real longitudinal scans. The end-systole task produced clinical errors (incomplete septum, extra blob). No privacy test. Its image-quality scores were weaker than the Xia et al. baseline, which tracked age less accurately.
Why it matters for my thesis: Your template for checking that conditioning worked, using an independent regressor on the generated images.

Paper: Li et al. (2025). Phenotype-guided generative model for high-fidelity cardiac MRI synthesis. arXiv:2505.03426.
What it does: Generates cine CMR sequences that match a chosen set of cardiac phenotypes, then uses them to expand pretraining data.
Conditioned on: Cardiac phenotypes (the survey lists 82, such as LVEF and LVEDV).
Model: Two stages: a generative model for phenotypes, then a masked autoregressive diffusion model conditioned on them.
Data: UK Biobank (the survey gives 32,444 cine) plus a private dataset.
How it was evaluated: FID and Frechet Video Distance (per the survey). Downstream diagnosis and phenotype prediction.
Main finding: Pretraining on the synthetic data improved diagnosis and phenotype prediction on public and private data.
Limits / gaps: No privacy evaluation reported (per the survey). Phenotypes come from the images themselves, not from demographics.
Why it matters for my thesis: Shows clinical characteristics can be used as conditioning for cine CMR.
How well I checked it: Read the abstract. Numbers and evaluation details come from the Simula survey table.

Paper: Skorupko et al. (2025). Fairness-aware data augmentation for cardiac MRI using text-conditioned diffusion models. arXiv:2403.19508.
What it does: Generates extra cardiac MR images for under-represented groups so that a classifier becomes less biased.
Conditioned on: Text built from patient metadata (sex, age, BMI, health condition) plus cardiac geometry from segmentation masks.
Model: ControlNet on a denoising diffusion model (Stable Diffusion based). Run on one consumer-level GPU.
How it was evaluated: Realism with established metrics, then a downstream classification test.
Main finding: Reduced imbalance, for example scarce diagnosed female patients and normal-BMI patients with heart failure.
Limits / gaps: No privacy test (the survey only notes it mitigates privacy and fairness issues). Needs UK Biobank access.
Why it matters for my thesis: The closest published work to 'clinical profile plus mask'. Your thesis adds a direct check of the conditioning and a full fidelity, utility and privacy comparison.
How well I checked it: Read the abstract. Details come from the Simula survey table.

Paper: Hosseini and Serag (2025). Is synthetic data generation effective in maintaining clinical biomarkers? Front Artif Intell.
What it does: Tests whether diffusion-generated images keep the hidden features a classifier needs to recognise disease.
Data: Lung and retinal images. Not cardiac MRI.
How it was evaluated: A classifier trained to detect preserved biomarkers (F1 and AUC of 0.8 to 0.99).
Main finding: Diffusion models kept key features such as lung markings and retinal abnormalities.
Why it matters for my thesis: Supports your point that a realistic-looking image is not enough. Keep it out of any claim about cardiac MRI.

Paper: Edirisooriya et al. (2026). Balancing fidelity, utility, and privacy in synthetic cardiac MRI generation: a comparative study. arXiv:2603.04340.
What it does: Generates masks first, then images from the masks. Compares three image generators on fidelity, segmentation utility and privacy.
Model: Mask generation with a DDPM. Image generation with a DDPM, a latent diffusion model, and flow matching with ControlNet.
Data: ACDC (150 subjects) and M&Ms (375). 2D slices at 128x128.
How it was evaluated: Fidelity: SSIM, MS-SSIM, PSNR, FID, KID, LPIPS. Utility: DynUNet segmentation tested across datasets (Dice, IoU, HD95, ASD). Privacy: nearest-neighbour distance and membership inference attack.
Main finding: DDPM gave the best balance. Flow matching looked promising for privacy but scored slightly lower on the task. Membership-inference AUC was 0.58 to 0.60 for all three. Real-data Dice was 0.90 to 0.93, against 0.82 to 0.90 for synthetic.
Limits / gaps: Conditions on masks only, with no clinical profile. Small datasets and 128x128 images.
Why it matters for my thesis: Your evaluation protocol, and a likely source for your baseline. Co-authored by Vajira Thambawita.

Paper: Cao et al. (2026). Anatomy-guided residual motion diffusion for controllable 4D cardiac MRI synthesis. arXiv:2606.26764 (also listed on the MICCAI 2026 papers site).
What it does: Generates 4D cine CMR together with matching segmentation masks for a chosen clinical profile. Separates static anatomy from motion.
Conditioned on: Clinical priors: diagnosis category, slice count, and end-diastolic, end-systolic and ejection-fraction volumes.
Model: Semi-supervised 3D VAE-GAN (image and mask decoders), a latent diffusion model for end-diastole anatomy, and a second latent diffusion model for residual motion. An MLP embeds the clinical priors and they enter by cross-attention.
Data: Training: 100 labelled ACDC patients plus 856 unlabelled Kaggle Data Science Bowl patients. Tests: ACDC test set, M&Ms (134 patients) and M&Ms-2 (157 patients).
How it was evaluated: FID and Frechet Video Distance. Pearson correlation between the clinical priors given and the volumes measured on the generated data. Segmentation (nnU-Net, UNETR, Swin-UNETR) trained on 900 synthetic pairs, scored with Dice and Hausdorff distance.
Main finding: FID 72.21 and FVD 288.08. Conditioning check gave r between 0.66 and 0.94. Adding synthetic data raised cross-vendor Dice by 1.4% on average and cut Hausdorff distance by 3.0 mm with nnU-Net.
Limits / gaps: No privacy evaluation. Higher guidance scales kept the volume trend but drifted from the exact target value. Conditions on diagnosis and volumes only, not age or sex.
Why it matters for my thesis: The closest published work to your thesis: clinical-profile conditioning, paired image and mask, and a check that the conditioning worked. Your thesis differs by comparing against a no-conditioning baseline and by testing privacy. Worth citing and positioning against.

Paper: Fang et al. (2026). ECGFlowCMR: pretraining with ECG-generated cine CMR helps cardiac disease classification and phenotype prediction. KDD 2026. arXiv:2601.20904.
What it does: Generates cine CMR from a patient's 12-lead ECG and uses the synthetic videos to pretrain disease and phenotype models.
Conditioned on: The patient's 12-lead ECG (a clinical signal, not demographics).
Model: Phase-aware masked autoencoder for the ECG, then a 3D-VAE anatomical template with DiT-based flow matching for motion.
Data: UK Biobank plus a proprietary clinical dataset of 535 patients.
How it was evaluated: LPIPS, FID, FVD and inference time. Downstream disease classification, phenotype prediction and an external transfer test.
Main finding: Reported FID 37.28 and FVD 14.41, better than the baselines in its table. Synthetic pretraining gave small but steady gains, roughly 1 percentage point, in the mixing-ratio tables.
Limits / gaps: The ECG constrains anatomy only weakly, which the authors note themselves. I did not see a privacy test. Part of the data is proprietary.
Why it matters for my thesis: A different kind of patient-specific conditioning. It also argues that CPGG is limited because it needs phenotypes extracted from CMR segmentations.
How well I checked it: Read the main text and tables. Did not read the appendix or limitations section.

Paper: Kumarasinghe et al. (2026). Synthetic cardiac MRI image generation using deep generative models. arXiv:2603.24764.
What it does: Reviews GAN, VAE, diffusion and flow-matching approaches to CMR generation through fidelity, utility and privacy.
Conditioned on: Covers unconditional, mask-conditioned and covariate-conditioned models.
Data: Includes tables of CMR datasets and of published generation models.
How it was evaluated: Not applicable. It compares what other papers reported.
Main finding: Privacy is rarely evaluated. Cross-dataset testing is rare, and when done (ACDC to M&Ms) it shows big drops. Pathology-specific mask-conditioned generation is limited.
Limits / gaps: A review, so no new experiments. I could not find 'personalization' discussed in the version I read (see the Check sheet).
Why it matters for my thesis: Backs up your gap statements on privacy and cross-dataset evaluation. Its Table III lists Campello, Li and Skorupko as the covariate-conditioned examples.
